serpGaps: Nearly every ranking page compares app DEVELOPMENT vendors (lowcode.agency, dribbble content hub, buildfire, propelrr, weareaffective). Codewave's page is the only design-specific one, it is dated February 2024, and its snippets stay generic (cost, flexibility, marketplaces). No page breaks a mobile app design project into the skills it needs and shows which of them one person usually covers.

No page addresses the two-platform problem: designing to Apple HIG and Material Design 3 at once (touch targets 44x44 pt vs 48x48 dp, tab bar vs navigation bar, back navigation). This is the clearest mobile-specific reason the choice changes, and Google publishes an official iOS-to-Android translation guide to cite.
No page says who recruits and runs user tests in each model, though testing a prototype before code is the main way mobile design lowers rework.
No page covers life after handoff: reviewing the first TestFlight and Google Play Console test builds against the design, and whether a freelancer is still available then.
The pages compare hourly rates, but no page compares calendar time (one person working in sequence vs a team working in parallel) for the same scope.

Portfolio advice is spread over separate dev-agency pages (lowcode.agency portfolio checklist, dribbble, phenomenonstudio FAQ). No comparison post gives a hands-on 'install their apps on your phone' test that works for freelancers and agencies alike.
Agency pages argue only for agencies. No page routes the reader honestly (when a freelancer is the better buy) and then shows how to make quotes comparable line by line.

outline.h2: Is a freelancer or an agency better for mobile app design?
outline.answerHint: Neither by default. The answer depends on three things: how many platforms the app ships on, how many rounds of user testing it needs, and who will review the build after handoff. Price against quality is the wrong axis.
points: Intro (contrarian take, see variety): the usual framing is price against quality. A strong freelancer often designs screens as good as an agency's, so the real difference is in the work around the screens. Then say what this post covers.
Answer the H2 in one bold sentence (a direct answer, without a Yes/No opener, because this is a 'which' question).
Link UP to the hub early with the anchor 'mobile app UI UX design services'.

Scope sentence: this post compares design providers for an iOS and Android app. Generic freelancer vs in-house vs agency hiring is covered on the homepage comparison, so do not rebuild that table here.

outline.h2: What work sits inside a mobile app design project?
outline.answerHint: Six kinds of work: research, user flows, interface design, a tested prototype, a UI kit for both platforms and developer handoff. A solo freelancer is usually strong in two or three of them.
points: Do NOT re-list the hub's 6 deliverables with their descriptions. Frame the section by SKILL (researcher, interaction/UX designer, UI designer, test moderator, platform specialist, handoff/spec owner) and deep-link to the hub section #what-does-mobile-app-ui-ux-design-include for the deliverables.

Visual: a skill-coverage map. Rows are the 6 skills, and the columns are 'typical solo freelancer' and 'agency team'. Shade strong / partial / usually missing, and label it 'pattern, not a rule'. Its text goes behind 'Show as text'.
Honest note: some freelancers are excellent researchers, so the reader should ask which of the six a candidate covers instead of assuming.

outline.h2: Can one freelance designer cover both iOS and Android?
outline.answerHint: Yes, if they have shipped apps on both platforms and design each one to its own guidelines: Apple HIG on iOS and Material Design 3 on Android. Many freelancers design iOS first and stretch the same screens onto Android.
points: Boolean H2, so the answer starts with 'Yes'.

Concrete differences, citing the guidelines: minimum touch target 44x44 pt (Apple HIG) vs 48x48 dp (Material Design 3), tab bar vs navigation bar, system back navigation on Android, date pickers. These match the hub's UI kit and FAQ wording.

Cite Google's official guide to translating iOS designs to Android (developer.android.com). Do not copy its 10 steps; use it as the source for the point that the translation is planned work, not a reskin.
Test for the buyer: ask a freelancer for the Android version of one iOS project in their portfolio.
Visual: a platform pair card with 5 component pairs (iOS on the left, Android on the right) and the touch-target sizes. Its text goes behind 'Show as text'.
If the reader ships to the App Store only, link once to iOS app design services (the single allowed cross-hub link).

outline.h2: Who runs user testing when a freelancer designs your app?
outline.answerHint: Usually you do. Most freelance quotes cover the design hours, while recruiting participants, moderating sessions and writing up findings fall to the client unless the quote names them.
points: Our way (hub wording): a clickable app prototype is tested with 5 users per round, in Maze or in moderated sessions, before developer handoff. Cite Nielsen Norman Group's 'test with 5 users' article as the reason for rounds of 5.
Questions to put to either provider: who recruits, who moderates, how many rounds, and what the output is (findings plus the changed screens).
Keep it to a short paragraph and 4 bullet questions. No table here.

outline.h2: What happens at developer handoff and the first test build?
outline.answerHint: Handoff is where the two models differ most. The design has to reach developers as specs they can build in Swift, Kotlin, React Native or Flutter, and someone has to check the first TestFlight and Google Play Console test builds against it.
points: Our step 5 (hub): Figma files, specs and assets go to the developers, and we review the first TestFlight and Google Play Console test builds. Deep-link to the hub section #how-does-the-mobile-app-ui-ux-design-process-work.
Freelancer risk: the contract often ends at file delivery, and the person has moved to the next client by the time the build arrives. Ask for build review in writing.
One design for React Native or Flutter: link to the hub FAQ instead of re-answering it.
Stay silent on whether the agency also writes the code (see notes: conflict).

outline.h2: Same app, two plans: how do the timelines compare?
outline.answerHint: On the same scope, a solo freelancer works in sequence while a team runs research, UI and testing side by side, so the calendar time differs even when the hours are similar.
points: Visual (before/after style): twin timeline for an ILLUSTRATIVE 6-flow iOS and Android app. Top track: one freelancer, with phases in a row. Bottom track: an agency team, with phases overlapping over 4-8 weeks (hub timeline: discovery 3-5 days, flows and wireframes 5-10, prototype and testing 5-10, visual UI 5-10, handoff 2-5). Label the freelancer track 'illustrative, varies by person'. Its text goes behind 'Show as text'.
Do not invent a freelancer duration as a fact. Present it as the sum of the same phase lengths with no overlap, and say so.
Mention continuity: a solo designer's illness or a new client pauses the whole timeline.

outline.h2: How do you test a designer's mobile portfolio on your own phone?
outline.answerHint: Install 2-3 of their shipped apps from the App Store and Google Play and spend 20 minutes on them. Check the touch targets, back navigation, larger text settings and the empty and error states, then read one case study for its scope and results.
points: Visual: a 'phone in hand' checklist card with 8 checks. Its text goes behind 'Show as text'.

Case-study bar: a useful case study states the scope, platforms, problem and measured results. Show this with OUR real case studies and their exact numbers only (see notes), e.g. TradeZella: web and mobile app design in scope, user interaction +40%, user retention +25%. Anyday App: mobile wallet revamp, employee satisfaction +40%, 14 hours saved per week. Use these as DOWN links (max 2 in the body).
Do not attribute the case-study results to design alone; write 'after the revamp' and keep each client's own wording.
Dribbble-only shots without shipped apps are a weak signal for both freelancers and agencies. Say this without naming the platform negatively.

outline.h2: When should you hire a freelancer, and when an agency?
outline.answerHint: Hire a freelancer for a single-platform app with a few flows, a fixed visual brief and a product manager who can run testing. Hire an agency when the app ships on iOS and Android, needs tested flows before code, or has a launch date the whole team depends on.
points: Visual: a decision tree with 4 questions (platforms? tested before code? someone in-house runs testing and handoff? hard launch date?) leading to 'freelancer', 'freelancer + your PM' or 'agency'. Its text goes behind 'Show as text'.

Give 3 honest freelancer situations (e.g. a UI refresh of an existing app with a working design system, a single-flow feature, a clickable investor demo) and 3 agency situations. Each line names the situation and the reason, and no line is a straw man.
Stage note: freelancer for a demo now, agency once the app ships on both stores. Avoid copying the generic 'MVP favours freelancers' line from lowcode.agency.

Lead moment 1: the reader recognises a two-platform, tested-before-code case. Writer adds one specific invitation in site wording, e.g. 'we run this as a 4-8 week engagement that ends with a review of your first test builds'.

outline.h2: How do you compare a freelancer's quote with an agency's?
outline.answerHint: Put both quotes on the same lines: platforms, flows, test rounds, UI kit, app store assets and post-handoff build review. Price the lines the freelancer leaves out (recruiting, moderation, Android variants) before you compare totals.
points: Visual: a line-item comparison card with 7 lines, where each line marks 'in quote / not in quote / your cost'. No market prices. Its text goes behind 'Show as text'.

State our range once: $25,000-$60,000 for 4-8 weeks, driven by flows, platforms, test rounds and UI kit size. Deep-link to the hub #how-much-does-mobile-app-ui-ux-design-cost and do not restate the MVP/full examples from the hub.

Hourly vs fixed: an hourly quote moves with revisions, while a fixed-scope proposal names its lines. Do not quote any freelancer hourly rate unless the fact-checker verifies a named source (see notes).
Lead moment 2 (main offer, see leadAngle). Second UP link to the hub near the end. Close with the next step to /contact/.

faqs.q: Is a freelancer cheaper than an agency for mobile app design?
faqs.hint: Usually per hour, not always per project. Explain the hidden lines (recruiting and moderating tests, Android variants, build review) and point to the quote-comparison section. Give no market rates.

faqs.q: Can I start with a freelancer and switch to an agency later?
faqs.hint: Yes. Ask the freelancer for organised Figma files and a component library you own, so the next team inherits them. A mobile app redesign starts with a review of the current app (hub FAQ wording).

faqs.q: Do I need an in-house designer instead?
faqs.hint: Only when design work never stops. For a first app project, an outside team or freelancer is faster to start. Keep it to 2-3 sentences and do not rebuild the homepage comparison table.

faqs.q: Should the same designer do the iOS and the Android version?
faqs.hint: Yes, when they design each platform to its own guidelines from one shared user flow map (hub wording). Otherwise the Android app ends up as a stretched copy of the iOS app.

faqs.q: What should a mobile app design contract include?
faqs.hint: Platforms, flows, test rounds, deliverables (Figma files, UI kit, app store assets), ownership of files, and build review after handoff. Give no legal advice.
